content:

Welcome back.

Breakthroughs don’t come from hard work. Lots of people are willing to work hard.

The definition of unreasonable effort is that people who are willing to work hard think you’re focusing on the wrong thing, or allocating too much time and focus on it.

We won’t know if our unreasonable effort is justified until after it pays off. That’s one more reason why breakthroughs are scarce.

title: Heat Can Kill. It Can Also Heal
content:
Human beings don’t like heat. Particularly intense, extreme, prolonged heat. This year the European heat wave ruined vacations for thousands of travelers when temperatures exceeding 104 degrees Fahrenheit made it impossible to be outside. It also caused about 10,650 excess deaths over the course of one week in June, according to the World Health Organization. Before this summer, a 2024 paper published in the _Journal of the American Medical Association_ estimated that the number of heat-related deaths in the United States more than doubled between 1999 and 2023—rising from 1,069 to 2,325.

External heat kills by dehydration and heart overload. To cool down, the brain widens blood vessels near the skin, which forces the heart to beat faster. Heavy sweating drains the body of water and salt. Blood volume drops and so does blood pressure, starving organs of oxygen and causing the kidneys to shut down. The intestines can lose their own blood flow, which loosens the tight linkage between gut cells. Gut lining starts to leak harmful bacteria into the bloodstream, triggering systemic inflammation and shock. Overall, extreme heat kills more people than any other extreme weather events. Researchers in 2019 found that more people take their own lives during hot weather, too.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

Humans don’t like fevers, heat emanating from inside, either. Known by the technical term “hyperpyrexia,” fevers above 106.7 degrees F can kill you. At that temperature, you literally begin to cook. Cellular and structural proteins start to unfold, or in scientific terms, denature. Enzymes, proteins that drive chemical reactions in the body, also lose their shape. Cells can’t perform their normal metabolic activities, so they die en masse, leading to tissue breakdown and organ collapse. Whether external or internal, overheating a human body can be a dangerous endeavor.

And yet, emerging research finds that periodically and strategically subjecting humans to intense, but controlled heat offers a plethora of benefits. In modern medical contexts, extreme hypothermia has been used and studied for more than 50 years to treat certain types of cancer. And researchers have studied gentler versions of hyperthermia for about a decade in the treatment of depression. Even more surprisingly, scientists recently found that systematic, temporary exposure to high heat may protect against Alzheimer’s disease, likely by altering the function of proteins involved in brain glucose metabolism. Milder sweltering of human bodies—by way of saunas or hot baths—results in cardiovascular and immune benefits; it also might reduce inflammation and maybe even contribute to longevity. Moreover, some experts believe that regular exposure to intense heat can help humans develop a better cooling ability, which on a rapidly warming planet would go a long way.

**TRÈS CHAUD:**Europe baked in an unprecedented heat wave this summer, with towns like Lille, in northern France, feeling little respite in the evenings. _Credit: Lamiot / Wikimedia Commons_

As a young cardiologist in Finland who loved running and skiing, Jari Laukkanen often enjoyed a post-exercise sauna. “I had always such good feeling after this session, combining exercise and sauna, and then I started to think whether it would be possible to study if there’s some real effect on your body, mind, and cardiovascular system.” Sauna is a staple of Finnish culture, so Laukkanen had easy access to study subjects. He has been studying the beneficial effects of sauna for more than 15 years and is currently writing a book on the subject.

The most obvious benefits of sauna are cardiovascular. As heat increases blood flow to the skin, the heart beats faster and blood vessels dilate—causing a drop in blood pressure. Other forms of periodic heat, whether infrared, sauna, or hot baths, seem to have similar healthful effects. Rebekah Lucas, a researcher at the University of Birmingham, who published a 2025 review of more than 50 papers on the effect of various heat therapies on cardiovascular function, found that the source of heat is almost agnostic to its benefits.

Both Lucas and Laukkanen found that regular heat immersion may also reduce arterial stiffness and improve the function of the inner linings of blood vessels, leading to lowered blood pressure over time—in part because increased body temperature mimics to some extent what happens during exercise. That’s not to say that sauna is a replacement for exercise, cautioned Laukkanen. “Sauna does not involve the same skeletal muscle activity or energy expenditure.”

Laukkanen has also found that heat stimulates the immune system. In a study published in March, he measured immune responses in people after a 30-minute sauna session, and observed increased activity in leukocytes, the white blood cells that protect your body from infections. In another study, he found that regular sauna use reduced levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of systemic inflammation in the body. “These findings suggest that heat can influence immune system activity,” he said, “although this does not establish that sauna bathing _directly_ lowers CRP or reverses inflammation.” It’s likely a complex interplay of various biological processes.

Because targeted heat can alter immune function and inflammation, anecdotal evidence points to a potential benefit of hyperthermia therapy combined with antibiotics to treat the symptoms of Lyme disease. Some private clinics and hospitals in the U.S. and abroad offer hyperthermia in the treatment of “chronic Lyme,” a controversial diagnosis in and of itself. Some Lyme disease sufferers report experiencing symptoms of the infection for years after their initial tick bites. While proponents of chronic Lyme hold that these lingering symptoms result from recalcitrant pockets of _Borrelia burgdorferi_, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, more-mainstream scientists contend that these symptoms are caused by the inflammatory havoc wrought by the pathogen.

Either way, the parents of Gregory Kotlyarsky heard of St. George Hospital in Bad Aibling, a city in southern Germany, in 2023 and decided that using hyperthermia could help their son, who they believed was suffering from chronic Lyme.

Kotlyarsky was first diagnosed with Lyme as a teenager in New York State, where he grew up. “I was bitten by a tick,” he recalled, but his symptoms weren’t terrible—a skin rash and headaches. A course of antibiotics seemed to help, and he forgot all about it. As a young man, he was healthy enough to serve in the National Guard for two years. He was thinking about going to college too.

It was during his National Guard training that Kotlyarsky’s symptoms came back, even though he was sure he wasn’t bitten again. “I was so paranoid about ticks that I always checked myself,” he said.

Gregory did another blood test, but while he waited for the results, he felt better, so he missed the message from his doctor’s office telling him he tested positive for Lyme again—and went without treatments for a while.

Eventually, his headaches returned, now accompanied by extreme anxieties. He left the National Guard. Blood work suggested he still had Lyme. When it became clear that antibiotics weren’t helping his symptoms, Kotlyarsky’s parents looked for alternatives—and found the German clinic through word of mouth and internet search. Both parents had engineering degrees, so the science made sense to them too. _B. burgdorferi_, like most organisms, is sensitive to heat. It starts to die at 104.9 degrees F, but to kill it entirely, it must be heated to 107.2 degrees F, the clinic’s doctors explained. “We go a little higher to 41.8 degrees C [107.2 degrees F], because the higher you go, the more aggressive the heat is on the biological level,” said Martin Rößner, the clinic’s chief physician. “We also combine it with antibiotics, and due to the heat, the responsiveness to the antibiotics is increased.”

The high temperature increases blood circulation, and also causes the breakdown of bacterial biofilms—microbial communities that clump together under normal conditions, making them harder to kill. To date, the clinic has treated 12,000 patients for chronic Lyme, according to its website. Assured that the procedure was done under intensive care unit-like conditions, the Kotlyarsky family felt it was worth trying. “I was mostly hoping that I would wake up and feel better right away,” Gregory Kotlyarsky said—even though doctors had told him he would likely notice the difference a few months later. He wasn’t scared of the dangerous temperatures to which he would be subjected for several hours. “I wasn’t afraid,” he said. “I just wanted to be treated and move on.”

So in January of 2024 he fell asleep, sedated, underneath an array of infrared lamps, hooked up to an IV that pumped antibiotics into his veins, envisioning waking up with the Lyme bacteria dying off inside him.

Outside the contentious use of hyperthermia in Lyme treatment, researchers have shown that heat can offer mental health benefits. Charles Raison, professor of human ecology and psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, reported in a 2016 paper treating patients with major depressive disorder using a milder form of hyperthermia, heating them only to only 101.3 degrees F during a single session that could run from less than an hour and a half to more than two hours. The study had two cohorts, subjects that actually received the hyperthermia treatment and a sham one, in which participants were heated only slightly, but they believed they were getting full exposure. Many participants in the hyperthermia group noticed the effects quickly. “A lot of people felt better, less depressed, within a day or two,” said Raison. Some felt better for two or three weeks. “And there were a couple of people that went into remission, meaning people who had failed antidepressants, who months later still felt better.”

Credit: Galyna Andrushko / Envato

Exactly how hyperthermia might alleviate depression is somewhat of a mystery, but Raison hypothesized that heat-sensitive nerves in our skin send messages to the brain’s mood-regulating circuits. “There are pathways from the skin to the brain that activate and go up into a serotonin area of the brain called the dorsal raphe nuclei,” he said, making the brain produce more serotonin, the “happiness hormone.”

Laukkanen’s lab has also reported a surprising finding involving heat therapy and mental health. In 2017, Laukkanen published a study that found that men who used a sauna four to seven times a week had more than 60 percent lower incidence of Alzheimer’s disease over 20 years compared to those who used it only once a week. Three years later, a study done by different Finnish researchers on men _and_ women suggested that regardless of sex, frequent sauna-goers enjoy a lower risk of dementia.

Molecular biology supports the relationship between heat and dementia protection. Researchers studying Alzheimer’s at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri, were surprised to learn that one of their participants, Doug Whitney, who carried a genetic mutation that predisposed him to developing Alzheimer’s in midlife, somehow dodged the bullet. Whitney was over 60 and had no symptoms, unlike most of his family members. The cause of that miracle may have been his unusual workplace. For decades, Whitney worked in the engine rooms of Navy ships, where temperatures can reach 122 degrees F. When researchers examined his blood, they found that he had extremely high levels of heat shock proteins—compounds that act like molecular chaperones to other proteins. They help proteins fold correctly and can even unfold misfolded ones. In Alzheimer’s, misfolded tau proteins underlie the disease, so researchers hypothesized that unusually high levels of heat shock proteins may have wielded a protective effect.

Doctors at St. George Hospital stumbled upon treating Lyme disease with heat by accident. And that chance discovery occurred at the intersection of the more-established use of heat therapy in treating cancer and its more controversial use in infectious disease.

In the 1990s, the clinic developed an integrative cancer treatment approach, in which conventional cancer therapies were combined with hyperthermia. Tumors are typically hypoxic, or starved of oxygen, overcrowded by their own rapidly dividing cells, and also acidic, all of which makes them more vulnerable to heat. On the contrary, healthy cells, which receive more oxygen and a richer nutrient supply, are better equipped to withstand such stressors. The combo of chemotherapy and heat produced better results than conventional treatments alone, and patients flocked to the clinic from all over the world.

Then in the early 2000s, the clinic had two patients with advanced breast cancer, one from the U.S. and one from Canada, who also suffered from recalcitrant Lyme disease. After undergoing hyperthermia for cancer, their Lyme symptoms disappeared, and their doctors took note.

The molecular dynamics underlying the potential benefit of heat may be similar between dementia and Lyme. Omar Morales, a doctor in Mexico who battled chronic Lyme and treated himself with hyperthermia, which he learned from the founders of the German hospital, explained that hyperthermia activates the heat shock proteins. “The heat causes the release of heat shock proteins that allow cells to mobilize,” Morales said, “and activate the adaptive immune system response, which is important for chronic conditions.” Heat also mobilizes T cells, immune cells that help the body fight infections.

Jake Scott, an infectious disease specialist at Stanford University School of Medicine, has been a vocal opponent of the chronic Lyme concept and the use of non-mainstream treatments, such as hyperthermia, to treat lingering Lyme symptoms. “The term ‘chronic Lyme disease’ isn’t supported by current medical evidence,” Scott said in a statement last year. “When patients tell me about ongoing fatigue, pain, and cognitive difficulties, I believe them completely. These symptoms are real and debilitating. But the science shows us these aren’t caused by persistent Lyme bacteria, so we need to look for other treatable causes.” Despite a lack of support from Western medical professionals, established Lyme and infectious disease societies, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, several clinics continue to offer hyperthermia in the treatment of long-term Lyme symptoms. However, there may be some emerging evidence too: At a 2026 medical conference in Florida, a team of U.S. doctors reported successfully treating a case of Lyme using extracorporeal hyperthermia, in which the patient’s blood was channeled into a machine that heated it before circulating it back into the patient.

Most Lyme disease patients respond not immediately after heat therapy, but in a few months, Rößner said, because the body takes time to heal after Lyme’s damage. “Most of our patients, I would say, achieve 90 to 98 percent of recovery, going to the gym, returning to college, being able to have social life again, marry, have kids,” he said. “People who were completely out of life are going back to their life.”

Kotlyarsky had two hyperthermia sessions over two weeks, a standard course for the treatment. When he opened his eyes after the first session, he looked like he’d just gotten over a long illness, his parents recalled. “The first time I woke up hours after the procedure ended, I felt like somebody had knocked me out with a baseball bat,” Kotlyarsky said. “After the second one, I woke up right after the procedure, and I didn’t feel nearly as sick.” He said that he felt a significant improvement a few months later. His headaches eased and so did his anxieties. And although he still sometimes feels anxious, he is now able to take college courses, enjoy time with friends, and travel between New York City and New Hampshire, where his parents live.

Why don’t people die from hyperthermia therapies the same way they succumb to high fevers and overheating? Fevers or heat waves “don’t have an off switch,” Morales explained. If a person battling a dangerous fever arrives at a hospital, they likely won’t die. If a person experiencing a heat wave can shelter in an air-conditioned space, they won’t die either. But if they don’t have these options, their bodies will eventually break down. On the contrary, hyperthermia is done under medical supervision with patients’ vitals continuously monitored.

If periodic heat therapies offer so many benefits, are we missing out by not breaking a sweat? Should we be cranking up the heat on ourselves? Some experts think so, because being hot sets off an adaptive response. “It’s that idea of hormesis,” Raison said—the biological phenomenon that means what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger. Chronic stressors can destroy you, but stressors limited in time and intensity can paradoxically strengthen one’s system.

Can subjecting ourselves to reasonable heat stressors help us deal with heat waves on a rapidly warming planet? Raison said he believes it can. “If you want to help people tolerate heat, the way to do it is not to give them an ice pack. The way to do it is to put them in a very hot place,” he said—and regularly. The time-limited exposure to intense heat causes the body to recalibrate. “It allows the body to shed heat more easily. It enhances thermoregulatory cooling capacity,” he explained. That’s how the military trains soldiers to be deployed in hot climates, Raison added. In that vein, periodic heating would help bolster our own “thermoregulatory cooling resilience,” as he called it.

But can immersive heat extend our lifespans? “Aging involves gradual changes in vascular function, metabolic regulation, inflammation, cellular maintenance, and the body’s ability to respond to physiological stress,” said Laukkanen. “Repeated, appropriately controlled heat exposure may influence several of these processes” in a beneficial way.

So even while heat as a medical treatment continues to be studied and debated, it might pay to heat up and break a sweat. It may or may not make you live longer, but at least it could help build up your own thermoregulatory cooling resilience. And regular, controlled heat exposure just might make you more able to enjoy your summer vacation in Europe again. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Astronomers Have Found a Star System That “Should Not Exist”
content:
There are many oddities out in space—as David Bowie foretold—and astronomers have just discovered yet another: a triple-star system some 28 light-years from Earth that shouldn’t really exist in its current form.

For decades, experts thought this system contained only two star remnants. The data showed a red dwarf (the smallest type of hydrogen-burning star, significantly smaller than the sun) being orbited by a very distant white dwarf (the burnt-out remnants of a dead star, typically about the size of Earth).

**Read more: “**[**Did Astronomers Finally Witness a Black Hole Eat a White Dwarf for the First Time?**](https://nautil.us/did-astronomers-finally-witness-a-black-hole-eat-a-white-dwarf-for-the-first-time-1268498)**”**

What was hiding was another white dwarf much closer to the central red dwarf star. A reanalysis that started in 2019—and has now been [published](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202661214) in the journal _Astronomy & Astrophysics_—offers clues as to what exactly this unusual stellar system has in it. “We were actually looking for planets,” study author Étienne Artigau said in a [statement](https://exoplanetes.umontreal.ca/en/astronomers-discover-remarkable-triple-star-system-just-28-light-years-from-earth/). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”

Multiple telescope readings were combined to find all three stellar objects. _Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST/International Gemini Observatory/NSF_

The velocity changes of the red dwarf suggested that something with much more mass than an exoplanet was pulling on it, which is how the white dwarf was uncovered. While these white dwarf remnants are the size of Earth, they’re about 200,000 times heavier—entire stars crushed down into (relatively) tiny specks.

Why is all of this so unexpected?

Before this inner white dwarf became a white dwarf, it would’ve ballooned in size, becoming around 40 percent bigger than the sun. Under normal circumstances, that would have pulled in the red dwarf and swallowed it up. But somehow, the red dwarf beat the odds and is still there—though it’s not clear how. “The system should not exist,” study author Patrick Dufour [said](https://exoplanetes.umontreal.ca/en/astronomers-discover-remarkable-triple-star-system-just-28-light-years-from-earth/). “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”

The new triple-star system has been given the name Welopōʻai, which means “path of family traits” in Hawaiian—an acknowledgement to the two telescopes that made the discovery, both located on Maunakea on the Big Island.

It promises to be of great value in studying how different types of stars and their inner structures evolve, and how matter reacts when under extreme densities. After all, it’s the closest triple-star system including two white dwarfs that’s ever been discovered, and there’s no other system like it within 100 light-years of Earth. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# The Next Frontier for Cancer Research? Space

There may be no better environment to grow and study tumors

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

3:00 PM CST on November 27, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/01-cancer.jpg?w=2880)

Every time astronauts return home, scientists learn more about how being in space [affects human biology](https://nautil.us/the-most-fascinating-findings-after-a-quarter-century-of-science-in-the-iss-1245907). There’s also now increasing evidence that space can act as a special kind of laboratory for studying diseases, which is why cancer microtumors are being grown on board the International Space Station (ISS).

[Video 4](https://video.primis.tech/uploads/cn1/video/users/hls/29874/video_692301aa2ef9f064006191/vid69c98ee210bd6987690922.mp4/chunklist_480.m3u8)

It might sound counterintuitive, but cancer tumors grown in orbit more closely resemble those in the human body. The lack of gravity means they assemble into the right 3D shapes more readily, allowing researchers to get a better idea of how they spread—and how they react to treatment.

**Read more: “**[**How a Sick Chicken Revolutionized Cancer Research**](https://nautil.us/how-a-sick-chicken-revolutionized-cancer-research-1286219)**”**

Those are two aspects of cancer—how well people respond to chemotherapy, and how tumors metastasize—where there’s a lot of variability between patients. Better modeling of those variables in full microgravity 3D promises to improve approaches to tackling the disease. For instance, one of the aims is to cut down on the rounds of chemotherapy that patients need, as well as minimize side effects, by tailoring treatments more specifically.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

This particular experiment is called Encapsulate-1, named after the biotech company developing the technology. They biopsy samples from real patients to grow mini tumors on chips, which are then stored in a portable, self-contained, lunchbox-sized lab sent to the ISS. Encapsulate researchers on the ground monitor the development of the cells from Earth via camera feeds and other monitoring instruments.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMARJB_qyhw)

“The astronauts didn’t need to touch anything,” Encapsulate founder Armin Rad [told _Upward_](https://issnationallab.org/press-releases/your-tumors-best-treatment-a-space-based-test-could-tell-you/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the ISS lab magazine. “Honestly, they just plugged it in like a coffee machine.”

Encapsulate’s experiments are scheduled to run for three years, backed up by further research and development [in labs](https://today.uconn.edu/2026/08/exploring-precision-medicine-for-pancreatic-cancer/) still weighed down by Earth’s gravitational pull.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

It’s not just cancer tumors that are being grown in space either. There’s growing interest in manufacturing [cancer drugs there](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/04/us-firm-varda-space-industries-manufacturing-drugs-in-space) as well. Microgravity is again the reason, because the same lack of pressure and pull that helps tumors expand properly can also allow drug crystals to fully form.

It’s space exploration of a whole different kind. ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

### [Heat Can Kill. It Can Also Heal](https://nautil.us/heat-can-kill-it-can-also-heal-1287047)
From sauna sessions to hospital hyperthermia, it is emerging as a promising healing tool

title: This Ancient Egyptian Curse Ritual Ended Up in a Garbage Heap
content:
According to ancient Egyptian beliefs, every night the sun descended to the underworld ferried on a boat shepherded by the sun god Ra. During his nightly voyage, Ra was attacked by the great serpent Apophis, the embodiment of chaos and darkness. Though these two were locked in an eternal struggle, Ra managed to put up Harlem Globetrotters numbers against his age-old nemesis, emerging victorious against the serpent each morning.

Of course, he had a little help. As Ra journeyed through the underworld, Egyptian priests working topside performed a ritual designed to curse Apophis by stabbing, burning, and spitting on graphical and wax effigies of the serpent. Until recently, most of what was known about the ritual came from a single copy in a spellbook dated to the fourth century BCE. But according to a new study published in the _Journal of the Egyptian Language and Antiquities_ the Apophis curse ritual is older and more pervasive than previously thought.

**Read more: “**[**This Is What an Egyptian Mummy Smells Like**](https://nautil.us/this-is-what-an-egyptian-mummy-smells-like-1267440)**”**

Fredrik Hagen from the University of Copenhagen and a team of Egyptologists analyzed 40 fragments of papyrus excavated from a Temple garbage heap in the ancient city of Thebes. No bigger than postage stamps, these fragments appear to be mass-produced copies of the illustrations and scripts used in the ritual. Dated to around 3,400 years old, the fragments push back the earliest evidence of the ritual by a millennium.

“These tiny fragments give us a new indication of how widespread curse rituals were in ancient Egypt,” Hagen explained in a statement. “Our finds and the subsequent analysis of the ritual confirms that it was a regular part of temple life, but a quick look at references to the ritual in other contexts also show that it was widely used outside temples, and that it was a common feature of Egyptian culture more broadly.”

In fact, the curse ritual was used to target the pharaoh’s enemies, other people, and even more conceptual antagonists like poison and inclement weather. So why hasn’t more evidence of it surfaced? According to the team, destroying the papyrus was part of the process.

“The papyrus drawing was often completely destroyed during the ritual, when it was trampled on, spit on, pierced with a knife and ultimately burned,” Hagen said. “For the ritual to be successful, the materials had to be destroyed by fire, so we are extremely fortunate to have found any of them in a condition that still allows them to be recognized and studied.”

The ash heap of history turns out to be more interesting than previously thought. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

Thanks to everyone who entered or voted in the book review contest. The winners are:

*   **1st:**_**[The Epic Of Gilgamesh](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-epic-of-gilgamesh)**,_ reviewed by John Wendover. John is a machine learning engineer from the UK. He hasn't written much publicly before but has tentatively started a Substack, [Engines of Eudaimonia](https://johnwendover.substack.com/)

*   **2nd:**_**[Lee Kuan Yew’s Memoirs](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-lee-kuan-yews-memoirs)**_, reviewed by Shaked Koplewitz. Shaked is a quant trader and prediction market enthusiast living in New York. He blogs at [shakeddown](https://shakeddown.substack.com/about), and people who liked the book review may also like his [review of Singapore as a city](https://shakeddown.substack.com/p/country-review-post-singapore).

*   **=3rd:**_**[The Tale of Genji](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-tale-of-genji)**,_ reviewed by Jenni Juvonen. Jenni writes about her temporary hyperfixations in [New Question Detected](https://newquestiondetected.substack.com/) on Substack (including topics like mermaid composition and horror movie psychology), and will soon publish a response to the comments on the Genji review.

*   **=3rd:**_**[The Escape Artist](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-escape-artist)**,_ reviewed by Max Nussenbaum. Max writes at [Candy for Breakfast](https://www.candyforbreakfast.email/). You may remember him from such reviews as _[Public Citizens](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-public-citizens)_ and _[The Outlier](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-outlier)._

First place gets $2,500, second place $1,000, third places get $500 each. Email me at scott@slatestarcodex.com to tell me how to send you money; your choices are Paypal, Bitcoin, Ethereum, check in the mail, or donation to your favorite charity. Please contact me by December 10 or you lose your prize.

The other Finalists were:

*   _**[The Book of Abraham](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-book-of-abraham)**,_ reviewed by Marius Binner. Marius Binner is a PhD student in AI Safety from Norway. You can read his Substack [here](https://mariusbinner.substack.com/).

*   _**[Great and Desperate Cures](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-great-and-desperate)**,_ reviewed by John V. John is a neuroscientist and AI researcher in Boston; he also wrote previous finalists [How Language Began](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-how-language-began) and [The Synaptic Plasticity and Memory Hypothesis](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-review-the-synaptic-plasticity). He started blogging at _[Theories of Intelligence](https://theoriesofintelligence.substack.com/)_, and then took a long hiatus, but promises to actually start posting soon.

*   _**[Breakdown in Pakistan](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/breakdown-in-pakistan)**,_ reviewed by Joel Hafvenstein. Joel is an author and former development worker currently teaching geography in Kathmandu.

*   _**[A Residence of 21 Years in the Sandwich Islands](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21)**_, reviewed by Merrick Pierson Smela. Merrick is a biologist living in Boston. He leads research at [Ovelle Bio](https://ovelle.bio/), a startup he co-founded with the goal of growing human eggs from stem cells. He also writes about science on his blog [De Novo](https://denovo.substack.com/)

*   _**[Thomas Urquhart’s Translation of Rabelais](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-thomas-urquharts)**_, reviewed by Alex Z. Alex is a teacher and writer currently living in rural Missouri. He and some friends have a Substack called [Reading and Nothingness](https://readingandnothingness.substack.com/); he posts under the letter A. Topics right now are literature, philosophy, and related miscellany.

*   _**[This is Going to Hurt](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-this-is-going-to)**_, reviewed by an adversarial duo. Writer A is self_made_human, a transhumanist psychiatry trainee in the UK. He’s not entirely sure how he feels about living through Interesting Times. He’s open to job offers. He knows medicine and the LLMs that know it better (almost all of them). He blogs at [USSRI](https://substack.com/@selfmadehuman) and [LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/users/alphaandomega). Writer B is Van Occupanther, a psychiatrist from Australia and previous ACX book review finalist who will remain pseudonymous."

*   _**[We Present Television](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-we-present-television)**_, reviewed by Chris Finkle. Chris manages a library makerspace in Central Florida, where he spends most of his free time at various theme parks, haunts, and roadside attractions. He occasionally writes genre fiction and essays at [tereglith.substack.com](http://tereglith.substack.com/), and is very active on [letterboxd](https://letterboxd.com/tereglith/)

*   _**[Storm of Steel](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-storm-of-steel)**_, reviewed by Adrian Merritt. Adrian is a physicist in Germany working mainly on quantum materials and autonomous experimentation. He spends most of his free time chasing a three-year-old kindergartner around.

*   _**[The Ghost in my Brain](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-ghost-in-my)**_, reviewed by Rachel Calcott. Rachel is a PhD student studying minds at Harvard, and recently started blogging at [Drift Diffusion.](https://rachelcalcott.substack.com/) Since her review came out, she's built a website ([prototype](https://waythroughconcussion.org/)) that attempts to help people with persistent concussion symptoms navigate the maze of scientific literature on treatment; she hopes to expand this into a patient case registry and would welcome feedback

*   _**[The History and Adventures of an Atom](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-the-history-and)**_, reviewed by Hal Johnson. Hal substacks often at [Hal Johnson Books](https://haljohnsonbooks.substack.com/). He sincerely hopes anyone who enjoyed his writing will try some of the books he's written, all of which are available from your favorite(?) bookseller—maybe check out _[Impossible Histories](https://www.amazon.com/Impossible-Histories-Republic-President-Charlemagne-ebook/dp/B0BGDLJK9N/)_ (more-or-less nonfiction), _[Sudden Glory](https://www.amazon.com/Sudden-Glory-Hal-Johnson-ebook/dp/B0CCT4V4GC/)_ ("literary" fiction), or _[Immortal Lycanthropes](https://www.amazon.com/Immortal-Lycanthropes-Hal-Johnson-ebook/dp/B0D9376HQ2/)_ (YA fiction; remember when everyone was reading that?).

*   _**[Orality and Literacy](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-orality-and-literacy)**_, reviewed by Rain Oliver. Rain writes at [rainoliver.com](https://rainoliver.com/), and apart from this book review, the piece of writing he is most proud of having written this year is [this short story](https://rainoliver.com/threes-align).

I’m also giving out ten Honorable Mentions. These either came very close to making the finals, or had an interesting balance of very high and very low votes in the first round, or I just personally liked them. They are:

*   _**[Aesopian Language in Russian Literature](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/aesopian-language-in-russian-literature?q=aesopian)**_**,**reviewed by [didn’t answer my email requesting biographical details].

*   _**[That Hideous Strength](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/that-hideous-strength?q=that+hideou)**_, reviewed by FLWAB. He works in medical administration, and is studying to become a clinical psychologist; you can read his Substack [here](https://substack.com/@flwab/posts).

*   _**[The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/the-life-changing-magic-of-tidying-up?q=life-changing)**_**,**reviewed by [Amanda Luce](https://amandaluce.substack.com/). Amanda writes Lucid Thoughts about home organization, MAiD, GLP-1s, and happenings in the rationalist community. After winning in 2024 for her horrifying review of [Two Arms and a Head](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-two-arms-and-a-head), she did something happy and cute this year..

*   _**[The Pillow Book](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/the-pillow-book?q=the+pillow)**_**,**reviewed by Optimized Sphere. Sphere is a professional robot torturer who acquired an obsession with early modern Japan by staring too deeply into the Naruto fanfiction abyss; the resulting fanfiction can be found [here](https://archiveofourown.org/users/optimal_stingray/works). They also shitpost at [gender-trash.tumblr.com](https://gender-trash.tumblr.com/).

*   _**[The Merry Wives of Windsor](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/the-merry-wives-of-windsor?q=merry+wives)**_**,**reviewed by John Ott. John is a poet and playwright who lives in New England. He writes about history at [World War Zero](http://worldwarzero.substack.com/)

*   _**[Why Greatness Cannot be Planned](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/why-greatness-cannot-be-planned-by-joel-lehman-and-kenneth-stanley?q=why+greatness)**_**,**reviewed by Peter Curry. Peter writes about neuroscience, cognitive science and AI at [King Canute](http://kingcnut.substack.com/). He also builds AI tools for thinking about the future at [Lucid Dot](http://luciddot.com/)

*   _**[The Disciplinary Revolution](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/the-disciplinary-revolution-calvinism-and-the-rise-of-the-state-in-early-modern-europe?q=disciplinary)**_, reviewed by Noah Swank. Noah describes himself as “a layabout in DC”; you can follow his writing at [https://x.com/_noah_swank](https://x.com/_noah_swank)

*   _**[Cultural Evolution](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/cultural-evolution?q=cultural+evolution)**_**,**reviewed by Joshua Ingle. Joshua writes rationalist-adjacent sci-fi and fantasy about high-stakes ethical crises that force characters to rethink their worldviews, and is pursuing a career in biosecurity. His books are at [joshuaingle.com/books](http://joshuaingle.com/books).

*   _**[The Sovereign Child](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/the-sovereign-child?q=sovereign+child)**_**,**reviewed by Richard Meadows. Richard is a dad who lives in New Zealand. He writes essays and reviews on his substack, [Deep Dish](https://thedeepdish.substack.com/), and co-hosts [Do You Even Lit](https://dyel.thedeepdish.org/), a book club podcast for reformed nonfiction supremacists.

*   _**[Sowing The Mustard Seed](https://acxreviews.robennals.org/reviews/dictator-book-club-yoweri-musevenis-sowing-the-mustard-seed?q=sowing+the+mus)**_**,**reviewed by David Cramer. David is an American working in the games industry in London. Email him at [emaildavidcramer@gmail.com](mailto:emaildavidcramer@gmail.com) if you want to talk about the business of video games, the London art scene or being a Latter-day Saint fan of ACX.

If you’re currently listed as [didn’t answer my email requesting biographical details], email me a sentence or two about you in the same format as the ones above at scott@slatestarcodex.com, and I’ll edit you in.

All winners and finalists get a free ACX subscription at the email I have on record for them. I think I’ve completed this step; if you can see [this post](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/hidden-open-thread-4545), you’ve successfully been converted to a paid subscriber. If you should have gotten the subscription but still can’t view that post when logged in using the email you sent me, let me know.

All winners and finalists also get the right to pitch me essays they want me to put up on ACX. Warning that I am terrible to pitch to, reject most things without giving good reasons, don’t pay you any money, and am generally described as awful to work with - but you can do it if you want!

Next year we’ll be going back to an Everything-Except-Book-Reviews contest, so get busy doing-something-other-than-reading to your things-which-aren’t-books!

My biggest tl;dr when it comes to possessions is that you DO actually know what matters and what doesn't. Seriously. YOU KNOW.

My stuff (including almost all my books!) has been in storage for the last ~2 years. I miss my books! There have been so many moments when I've thought, wow, I really want to re-read my comfort book right now. But it's in a box in my storage unit! Ugh!

I missed certain books so much that I spent money on a Kindle copy, just to read it again.

Meanwhile, I barely remember some other books. Although they survived my tidying festival and they still spark joy, the intensity is much lower. I certainly haven't "needed" to read them again in the last two years.

Separately, all my posters and wall decorations are also in various boxes. But there was one item, a clock, that I missed so much that I went to the storage unit, dug through 3 layers of boxes, and fished it out just to put it on my wall.

The revealed preference is strong, here. Which items would you hike out to your storage unit and dig through a ton of boxes to retrieve? Which books would you pay money to re-buy, just to read again? Keep those. The rest isn't nearly as important.

Different Worlds - others in my family have hoarding tendencies, but I've tried hard not to inherit that. When things got to the point that I had enough stuff in my one room that I was considering, huh, I could rent one of the storage units nearby - no, cut that thought, Too Much Stuff. Hector, we must not conserve! One of the cleaning frenzies involved schlepping over a dozen garbage bags worth of clothing and shoes to the donation bins...and that wasn't the first time. There was even one unplanned involuntary move that required leaving a bunch of my stuff behind forever, which I don't have an inventory of, but honestly I don't miss that either. A lot can be said on the magic of shelving units for making more space, but the point should never be freeing up space just to fill it with more crap later. That's The Container Store trap.

The equivalent ugh field for me is things stored on backup drives. Never went for the cloud storage thing, so it's all on physical media...on a tower I haven't booted in years, which has subsequently been buried under new hobby supplies. Not even sure it still runs. It's not physically impossible to just remove the drive and wire it externally, yet...blah. Eventually all those pangs of "it'd be neat to rewatch $ANIME again" or "I could replay $VIDEOGAME" or whatever fade into the background. Very important, but to a past version of me. We are always changing into new people day by day, it's important the current environment suits who we are in the present rather than the past.

# The Pain in You and the God in You: Carl Jung on the Relationship Between Psychological Suffering and Creativity

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 36: The Pain in You and the God in You: Carl Jung on the Relationship Between Psychological Suffering and Creativity](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/carljung_letters.jpg?fit=320%2C508&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Selected-Letters-1909-1961-Bollingen-General/dp/0691640300/?tag=braipick-20)

When AI first began colonizing language — which is still our best instrument for bridging the abyss between us, a container for thought and feeling that shapes the contents — I asked chatGPT to compose a poem about a solar eclipse in the style of Walt Whitman. It returned a ledger of cliches in rhymed couplets. Getting the form wrong — Whitman did not rhyme — seemed like an easy correction by a line of code. Getting poetry itself wrong was the interesting question, the question that gets at the heart of why we make poems (or paintings or novels or songs) — a question fundamentally about what it means to be human.

I asked an elder poet friend why she thought chatGPT rang hollow where Whitman could compact infinities of feeling in a single image, could unseat the soul in a word.

She paused, then said: “Because AI hasn’t suffered.”

On the one hand, this echoes [a dangerous myth](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/14/elizabeth-barrett-browning-art-suffering/): the archetype of the tortured genius handed down to us by the Romantics, who, cornered in their time and place, in a century of bloody revolutions, deadly epidemics, and punitive Puritanical norms, must have needed to believe that their suffering — those lives of poverty and privation, those ill-fated exercises in projection mistaken for love, all those premature deaths — was a fair price to pay for such creative volcanicity.

On the other hand, this is reality: Art is the music we make from the bewildered cry of being alive — sometimes a cry of exultant astonishment, but often a cry of devastation at the collision between our wishes and the will of the world. Every artist’s art is their coping mechanism for what they are living through — the longings, the heartbreaks, the triumphs, the wars within and without. It is these painful convolutions of the psyche — which used to be termed _neurosis_ at the dawn of modern psychotherapy, and which we may simply call suffering — that reveal us to ourselves, and it is out of these revelations that we create anything capable of touching other lives, that contact we call art.

Our power and our freedom lie in learning to neither negate our suffering nor romanticize it but to harness its catalytic power as a current passing through us to jolt us alive, then passing on and down into the ground of being.

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/carljung.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Modern-Man-Search-Soul-Jung/dp/1684226384/?tag=braipick-20)

Carl Jung

No one has refuted the myth of the tortured genius without negating the fact and fertility of suffering more pointedly than [Carl Jung](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/carl-jung/) (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who [thought deeply about the nature of creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/04/09/carl-jung-creativity/).

In 1943, a scholar of Kierkegaard asked Jung’s opinion of the relationship between “psychological problems” and creative genius. With an eye to Kierkegaard’s gift for [letting his anxiety fuel rather than hinder his creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/06/19/kierkegaard-on-anxiety-and-creativity/), Jung declares him a “whole” person and not “a jangling hither and dither of displeasing fragmentary souls,” and writes:

> True creative genius does not let itself be spoilt by analysis, but is freed from the impediments and distortions of a neurosis. Neurosis does not produce art. It is uncreative and inimical to life. It is failure and bungling. But the moderns mistake morbidity for creative birth — part of the general lunacy of our time.
> 
> 
> It is, of course, an unanswerable question what an artist would have created if he had not been neurotic. Nietzsche’s syphilitic infection undoubtedly exerted a strongly neuroticizing influence on his life. But one could imagine a _sound_ Nietzsche possessed of creative power without hypertension — something like Goethe. He would have written much the same as he did, but less strident, less shrill — i.e., less German — more restrained, more responsible, more reasonable and reverent.

[![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/SummerRedBird_suffering1.jpg)](https://almanacofbirds.org/)

Art from [_An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days_](https://almanacofbirds.org/), also available as a [stand-alone print](https://www.society6.com/a/products/bird-divinations-summer-red-bird-about-almanacofbirdsorg_print) and as [stationery cards](https://www.society6.com/a/products/bird-divinations-summer-red-bird-about-almanacofbirdsorg_cards?curator=brainpicker).

A century before Alain de Botton offered his [assuring perspective on the importance of breakdowns](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/13/alain-de-botton-normalcy-breakdown/), Jung weighs what makes suffering generative or degenerative:

> Neurosis is a justified doubt in oneself and continually poses the ultimate question of trust in [man](https://www.themarginalian.org/pronoun/) and in God. Doubt is creative if it is answered by deeds, and so is neurosis if it exonerates itself as having been a phase — a crisis which is pathological only when chronic. Neurosis is a protracted crisis degenerated into a habit, the daily catastrophe ready for use.

Jung considers the advice he would have given Kierkegaard about how to orient to his suffering, which was the raw material of his philosophical writings:

> It doesn’t matter what _you_ say, but what _it_ says in you. To _it_ you must address your answers. God is straightaway with you and is the voice within you. You have to have it out with that voice.

Couple with a forgotten young poet’s [extraordinary letter to Emily Dickinson about how to bear your suffering](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/08/11/anne-reeve-aldrich-emily-dickinson/), then revisit Kierkegaard himself on [the value of despair](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/06/10/kierkegaard-despair/).

# Nobel-Winning Biochemist Gerty Cori on the Single Most Important Element of a Meaningful Life

### By Maria Popova

We call it “the long run,” life, and spend it trying to understand what keeps us running, trying to run toward, to see the true goal through all the false trophies promised us by the merchants of approval and acclaim.

What keeps the body running is glycogen — the essential fuel of muscles. What keeps the soul running is a substance we must each synthesize out of the mystery we are. There are two kinds of running the soul does: running away from — our fears, our past, our mistakes — and running toward. The first kind is easier, for it is reflexive. The second kind is life’s most difficult, most rewarding work — to discover the track on which to run and its most authentic destination, to synthesize out of our dreams and desires the glycogen of a strong animating spirit to fuel the long run of a purposeful, substantive, meaningful life.

[![Image 33](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Red-HeadedWoodpecker_purpose.jpg?resize=680%2C1052&ssl=1)](https://almanacofbirds.org/)

Card from [_An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days_](https://almanacofbirds.org/), also available as a [solo print](https://www.redbubble.com/shop/ap/170095631).

Czech biochemist **Gerty Cori** (August 15, 1896–October 26, 1957) — the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in science, for her discovery of how glycogen works in the body — articulated with poetic precision the animating spirit of a purposeful life when she [appeared](https://beckerarchives.wustl.edu/FC053-S01-B01-F01) on Edward R. Murrow’s popular radio series _This I Believe_ in the late summer of 1952:

> The love for and dedication to one’s work seems to me the basis for happiness… For a [scientist], the unforgotten moments of life are those rare ones, which come after years of plodding work, when the veil over nature’s secret seems suddenly to lift and when what was dark and chaotic appears in a clear and beautiful light and pattern.

This clarity of vision is not singular to science. Pulsating beneath Cori’s words is the insistence that a meaningful life — one that makes the long run worthy of running — springs from devotion to work, any work, that parts the veil of meaninglessness to reveal a glimpse of some greater truth. The most alive people I know, whether they make postulates or poems, furniture or film, are animated by such devotion. It is the best antidote to the existential catatonia of cynicism and despair that leaves people too petrified to live up to and into their gifts. Cori observes:

> I believe that art and science are the glories of the human mind… Contemplation of the great human achievements through the ages is helpful to me in moments of despair and doubt. Human folly then seems less important… I believe that cynicism and despair and the straitjacket into which totalitarian systems try to force the human mind are inimical to first rate achievements in art and science.

Complement with pioneering astrophysicist Maria Mitchell on [the art of knowing what to do with your life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/01/19/maria-mitchell-purpose/), then revisit psychologist Carl R. Rogers on [the three elements of the good life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/10/05/carl-rogers-good-life/) and Victor Frankl on [the secret to success](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/05/05/viktor-frankl-success/).

title: The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love
content:
[![Image 1: The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/donaldhall_without.jpg?fit=320%2C479&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Without-Poems-Donald-Hall/dp/0395957656/?tag=braipick-20)

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on [why we fall and how we stay in love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/26/alain-badiou-in-praise-of-love/). “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist **Donald Hall** (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of [_Poetry_](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine) — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/donaldhall_janekenyon.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)

Donald Hall and Jane Kenyon

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of [uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/15/jane-kenyon-advice-on-writing/) — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in [“the bead of sensation”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/11/virginia-woolf-on-relationships-marriage/) that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

> Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the _New Yorker_. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … _what do you do?_”
> 
> 
> What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.
> 
> 
> What we did: love.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/themissingpiecemeetsthebigo23.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/12/the-missing-piece-meets-the-big-o-shel-silverstein/)

Art from [_The Missing Piece Meets the Big O_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/12/the-missing-piece-meets-the-big-o-shel-silverstein/) — Shel Silverstein’s allegory of the secret to lasting love

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing _Little Prince_ author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s [beautiful insistence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/01/what-is-love/) that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

> We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/sophieblackall_thingstolookforwardto_FallinginLove.jpg?resize=680%2C811&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/05/12/sophie-blackall-things-to-look-forward-to/)

Art by Sophie Blackall from [_Things to Look Forward to_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/05/12/sophie-blackall-things-to-look-forward-to/)

For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

> We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach on Eagle Pond. Soft moss underfoot sent little red flowers up. Ghost birches leaned over water with wild strawberry plants growing under them. Over our heads white pines reared high, and oaks that warned us of summer’s end late in August by dropping green metallic acorns. Sometimes a mink scooted among ferns… Jane dozed in the sun as I sat in the shade reading and occasionally taking a note in a blank book. From time to time we swam and dried in the heat.

Hall’s most piercing point is that the third thing, rather than being an extraneous adornment of the relationship, is a central form of companionship. But while it is indispensable, it is not irreplaceable — it doesn’t so much matter what the thing is, only that it is.

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/AchievingPerspective_MairaKalman.jpg?resize=680%2C533&ssl=1)

Art by Maira Kalman from [_Achieving Perspective_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/18/achieving-perspective/) for [_The Universe in Verse_](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/)

When a landfill leakage destroyed their beloved pond, Hall and Kenyon still had their other third thing — poetry. Reflecting on its [unparalleled power of perspective](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/18/achieving-perspective/), its power to connect and console in the face of life’s darkest moments, he writes:

> We lived in the house of poetry, which was also the house of love and grief; the house of solitude and art; the house of Jane’s depression and my cancers and Jane’s leukemia. When someone died whom we loved, we went back to the poets of grief and outrage, as far back as _Gilgamesh_; often I read aloud Henry King’s “The Exequy,” written in the seventeenth century after the death of his young wife. Poetry gives the griever not release from grief but companionship in grief. Poetry embodies the complexities of feeling at their most intense and entangled, and therefore offers (over centuries, or over no time at all) the company of tears. As I sat beside Jane in her pain and weakness I wrote about pain and weakness. Once in a hospital I noticed that the leaves were turning. I realized that I had not noticed that they had come to the trees. It was a year without seasons, a year without punctuation. I began to write “Without” to embody the sensations of lives under dreary, monotonous assault. After I had drafted it many times I read it aloud to Jane. “That’s it, Perkins,” she said. “You’ve got it. That’s it.” Even in this poem written at her mortal bedside there was companionship.

Hall’s 1999 poetry collection [**_Without_**](https://www.amazon.com/Without-Poems-Donald-Hall/dp/0395957656/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/without-poems/oclc/37579932&referer=brief_results)) is the breathtakingly beautiful record of that abiding companionship. Complement it with Anna Dostoyevskaya on [the secret to a happy marriage](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/15/anna-dostoyevsky-reminiscences-marriage/) and Wendell Berry on [what poetry teaches us about the secret of marriage](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/11/18/wendell-berry-poetry-marriage/) and Adrienne Rich on [honorable human relationships](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/02/adrienne-rich-honorable-human-relationship/).

# How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 40: How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/hebert_thanks1.jpg?fit=320%2C407&ssl=1)](https://www.acornpressoakland.com/the-book-of-thanks)

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are [entirely improbable](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/07/25/richard-dawkins-death/), that we [bless that bright improbability](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/12/31/some-blessings-to-begin-with/) with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, [the wanting monster](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/05/29/the-wanting-monster/) always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, [the cobalt eye of the scallop](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/06/21/scallop-eye/), [the golden fan of the gingko](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/09/23/ginkgo/), [the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/08/23/ghost-pipe/).

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

[![Image 41](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Poppies_Hebert.jpg?resize=680%2C528&ssl=1)](https://www.acornpressoakland.com/the-book-of-thanks)

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in [**_The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes_**](https://www.acornpressoakland.com/the-book-of-thanks) — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).
